I am trying to extract files in loop. There are some file in KB and some file in MB. When I tried to extract individually it works file, for approx 12MB file, docling takes roughly half an hour to extract. but for the same file, when I tried to extract with other files and folders, it hangs for 3 hours and later I dismiss the task.

**Answer**: The CLI already has a couple of controls that are meant to help exactly in this kind of situation: `--document-timeout`, `--num-threads`, and format filtering. You can combine them to avoid “one bad / heavy file blocks everything”.

Below is what you can do, based on the `convert` command implementation you’re using.

---

### 1. Set a per‑document timeout

The `convert` command takes a `document_timeout` option and passes it into the pipeline options for standard PDF/image processing:

```python
document_timeout: Annotated[
    Optional[float],
    typer.Option(
        ...,
        help="The timeout for processing each document, in seconds.",
    ),
] = None,
...
pipeline_options = PdfPipelineOptions(
    ...
    document_timeout=document_timeout,
)
```  
(see `convert` in `docling/cli/main.py`)

So, if one large/complex file is stalling the pipeline, you can cap how long Docling spends on it, **per document**, rather than letting your whole batch run indefinitely.

Example: limit each document to 600 seconds (10 minutes):

```bash
docling convert \
  --document-timeout 600 \
  --num-threads 4 \
  --from pdf \
  --to markdown \
  path/to/folder
```

When a document exceeds that timeout, it will fail and be counted as a failed conversion; the loop continues with the rest of the files because `convert_all(..., raises_on_error=abort_on_error)` only aborts early if you explicitly enable `--abort-on-error`:

```python
conv_results = doc_converter.convert_all(
    input_doc_paths, headers=parsed_headers, raises_on_error=abort_on_error
)
```

So make sure you are **not** using `--abort-on-error` if you want to skip problematic documents and continue with the rest.

---

### 2. Use multiple threads, but not too many

The CLI exposes `--num-threads` and passes it to `AcceleratorOptions`, which is then used by the pipelines:

```python
num_threads: Annotated[int, typer.Option(..., help="Number of threads")] = 4,
device: Annotated[
    AcceleratorDevice, typer.Option(..., help="Accelerator device")
] = AcceleratorDevice.AUTO,
...
accelerator_options = AcceleratorOptions(num_threads=num_threads, device=device)
...
pipeline_options = PdfPipelineOptions(
    ...
    accelerator_options=accelerator_options,
    ...
)
...
asr_pipeline_options = AsrPipelineOptions(
    accelerator_options=AcceleratorOptions(
        device=device,
        num_threads=num_threads,
    ),
)
```

If you run a big batch, try a **moderate** value (e.g. 4–8) that matches your CPU cores instead of something very large. Too many threads can cause thrashing and make everything “hang” even though it is just overloaded.

---

### 3. Restrict input formats and file discovery

When you pass a directory, `convert` recursively discovers files based on `--from` formats:

```python
if from_formats is None:
    from_formats = list(InputFormat)
...
for fmt in from_formats:
    for ext in FormatToExtensions[fmt]:
        for path in local_path.glob(f"**/*.{ext}"):
            ...
            input_doc_paths.append(path)
        for path in local_path.glob(f"**/*.{ext.upper()}"):
            ...
            input_doc_paths.append(path)
```

If you don’t specify `--from`, it will try **all supported formats**. That might be pulling in many more files than you realize (PDF, image, office docs, HTML, MD, audio, etc.), which can make a batch run look like it’s “stuck” for hours.

When testing or dealing with one problematic file mixed into a tree of many, restrict `--from` so only the relevant formats are processed, e.g.:

```bash
docling convert \
  --from pdf \
  --to markdown \
  path/to/folder
```

You can also start by isolating the large files (e.g. by moving them into a temporary directory or specifying them explicitly on the command line) and running them with a timeout.

---

### 4. Turn off the heavier components for debugging

Some pipeline components (OCR, table structure, enrichment models) are more expensive. You can turn them off selectively to see what is slowing you down and keep the batch from ballooning:

Relevant options in `convert`:

```python
ocr: bool = True,          # --ocr / --no-ocr
tables: bool = True,       # --tables / --no-tables
enrich_code: bool = False,
enrich_formula: bool = False,
enrich_picture_classes: bool = False,
enrich_picture_description: bool = False,
```

Try, for a problematic batch:

```bash
docling convert \
  --from pdf \
  --to markdown \
  --no-ocr \
  --no-tables \
  --document-timeout 600 \
  path/to/folder
```

If this runs quickly, then gradually turn things back on (tables, then OCR, then enrichments) to identify what specifically makes the 12 MB file heavy.

---

### 5. Ensure page batching is reasonable

The pipeline has a performance setting for page batching:

```python
page_batch_size: Annotated[
    int,
    typer.Option(
        "--page-batch-size",
        help=f"Number of pages processed in one batch. Default: {settings.perf.page_batch_size}",
    ),
] = settings.perf.page_batch_size,
...
settings.perf.page_batch_size = page_batch_size
```

If you have very large / many‑page PDFs, reducing `--page-batch-size` can help balance memory and responsiveness:

```bash
docling convert \
  --from pdf \
  --to markdown \
  --page-batch-size 2 \
  path/to/folder
```

---

### 6. Use logging to see what’s happening

The `--verbose` flag controls logging:

```python
if verbose == 0:
    logging.basicConfig(level=logging.WARNING, ...)
elif verbose == 1:
    logging.basicConfig(level=logging.INFO, ...)
else:
    logging.basicConfig(level=logging.DEBUG, ...)
```

Run with `-v` or `-vv` to see:

```bash
docling convert \
  -vv \
  --from pdf \
  --to markdown \
  --document-timeout 600 \
  path/to/folder
```

During a “hang”, logs will usually show whether it’s stuck on OCR, table detection, a specific backend, etc.

---

### Summary of a robust batch command

Putting this together, a good starting point for your described case would be:

```bash
docling convert \
  --from pdf \
  --to markdown \
  --document-timeout 600 \
  --num-threads 4 \
  --no-ocr \            # or leave OCR on if you need it, just test both
  --no-tables \         # turn back on later if required
  -v \
  path/to/your/root
```

## Reference Answer
You can control the number of worker threads (and device) in your Python code by passing an AcceleratorOptions instance to PdfPipelineOptions. Here's how you can adapt your code:

```python
import multiprocessing
from docling.datamodel.pipeline_options import PdfPipelineOptions, AcceleratorOptions
from docling.datamodel.base_models import InputFormat
from docling.document_converter import DocumentConverter, PdfFormatOption

pdf_options = PdfPipelineOptions(
    do_code_enrichment=True,
    do_ocr=True,
    do_table_structure=True,
    do_picture_classification=True,
    accelerator_options=AcceleratorOptions(
        num_threads=multiprocessing.cpu_count(),  # Use all CPU cores
        device='auto'  # Or 'cuda' for NVIDIA GPU, 'mps' for Apple Silicon, 'cpu' for CPU only
    )
)

converter = DocumentConverter(
    format_options={
        InputFormat.PDF: PdfFormatOption(pipeline_options=pdf_options)
    },
)
```

- `num_threads` sets how many threads Docling will use for extraction. A good default is `multiprocessing.cpu_count()` to match your CPU cores.
- `device` can be `'auto'` (let Docling pick), `'cuda'` (NVIDIA GPU), `'mps'` (Apple Silicon GPU), or `'cpu'`.

You can also override the thread count with the `DOCLING_NUM_THREADS` or `OMP_NUM_THREADS` environment variables if you don't set it in code.

The `AcceleratorOptions` class (located in `docling/datamodel/accelerator_options.py`) provides configuration options for hardware acceleration, including device selection settings (CPU, CUDA, MPS for Apple Silicon), GPU memory management options, batch size configurations, and multi-threading/processing settings.
